lessonTitle: Metabolic and Synthetic Functions of the Liver

blocks.text: A 44-year-old man with advanced cirrhosis arrives with swollen ankles, a distended abdomen full of fluid, and bruises on his forearms after minor knocks. These look like three unrelated problems, but all come from one organ failing to make proteins it normally exports into the blood.

blocks.markdown: **The hepatocyte as a factory.** The liver receives about 25% of cardiac output, roughly three quarters of it as nutrient-rich venous blood from the gut through the **portal vein** and the rest as oxygenated blood through the **hepatic artery**. Blood flows through **sinusoids** past hepatocytes, so every absorbed nutrient and toxin (apart from those taken up by lymph) is processed before reaching the systemic circulation. Hepatocytes carry out four broad kinds of work: **metabolism** of carbohydrate, fat and protein; **synthesis** of plasma proteins; **detoxification and excretion**; and **storage**. Resident macrophages called **Kupffer cells** clear bacteria and debris from portal blood.

blocks.title: Hepatic reserve and first-pass metabolism
blocks.text: First-pass metabolism is processing of absorbed substances by the liver before they reach the systemic circulation. Hepatic reserve is the large spare capacity of the liver: tests of synthetic function usually stay normal until a large fraction of functional hepatocytes is lost, which is why liver failure often presents late.

blocks.markdown:
**Carbohydrate metabolism.** After a meal, the liver stores glucose as **glycogen** (liver glycogen is about 100 g in an adult) and converts galactose and fructose into glucose-pathway intermediates. Between meals it releases glucose by **glycogenolysis**, then by **gluconeogenesis** from lactate, glycerol and amino acids once glycogen runs low. The liver therefore keeps plasma glucose steady for the brain.

**Lipid metabolism.** The liver makes cholesterol, assembles triglyceride into **VLDL** for export, and during fasting oxidises fatty acids to **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate) as fuel for brain and muscle. It also converts cholesterol to bile acids.

**Protein metabolism and ammonia.** Hepatocytes carry out deamination and transamination of amino acids. Ammonia released is toxic to the brain and is converted to **urea** in the **urea cycle**, which occurs only in the liver; urea is excreted by the kidney. In liver failure, ammonia and other gut-derived toxins accumulate and contribute to hepatic encephalopathy.

**Plasma protein synthesis.** The liver makes **albumin** (the main plasma protein, reference about 35-50 g/L, varying by laboratory), most clotting factors (fibrinogen, prothrombin and factors V, VII, IX, X and others), many transport proteins, complement components, and angiotensinogen. **Albumin** provides most of the plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure and carries bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium and drugs. Its half-life is about 20 days. **Factors II, VII, IX and X** require vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation; factor V does not. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), so a falling factor VII is the earliest sign of lost synthetic capacity.

**Detoxification.** Phase I reactions (mainly cytochrome P450 oxidation) add or expose reactive groups; phase II reactions conjugate them (glucuronidation, sulphation, glutathione) to make water-soluble products for bile or urine. The liver also inactivates steroid hormones and insulin.

blocks.title: Albumin after synthesis stops
blocks.prompt: Suppose hepatic albumin synthesis stopped completely in a patient whose albumin was 40 g/L. Taking the half-life as 20 days and ignoring changes in volume or loss, what would the concentration be after 30 days?

steps.text: Work out the number of half-lives elapsed.
Calculate the result and interpret: albumin falls slowly, so chronic synthetic failure shows as low albumin only after weeks.

blocks.caption: Which liver test answers which question (reference ranges vary between laboratories).
rows: Synthetic function (slow marker, half-life about 20 days)
Low in chronic liver disease; also low in nephrotic syndrome and inflammation
Synthetic function (fast marker, factor VII half-life about 6 hours)
Prolonged when synthesis fails or vitamin K is lacking
Hepatocyte injury (enzymes leak from damaged cells); ALT is more liver-specific
Cholestasis or biliary injury (ALP is also from bone)
Raised in biliary obstruction and infiltration
Raised in many conditions; see bile unit

blocks.title: Calculating an INR
blocks.prompt: A patient's prothrombin time is 21 s and the laboratory's mean normal prothrombin time is 12 s. With an International Sensitivity Index (ISI) of 1.0, what is the INR, and what does it suggest?

steps.text: Interpret: a value of 1.75 is well above the normal range of about 1.0. Prolongation reflects reduced factors II, V, VII, X or vitamin K deficiency; if it fails to correct after vitamin K, hepatocellular synthetic failure is likely.

blocks.answer: INR is 1.75, indicating a prolonged clotting time that could reflect impaired hepatic synthesis or vitamin K deficiency.

items: Metabolic: glycogen storage, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, VLDL assembly, cholesterol and bile acid synthesis, urea cycle.
Synthetic: albumin, clotting factors, transport proteins, complement, angiotensinogen.
Detoxification: cytochrome P450 oxidation and conjugation of drugs, steroid hormones and bilirubin; ammonia to urea.
Storage: glycogen, iron (ferritin), vitamins A, D, B12 and K-related stores.
Immune: Kupffer cells clear bacteria and debris from portal blood.

blocks.title: Two kinds of liver test
blocks.text: Tests of injury (ALT, AST) and cholestasis (ALP, GGT) tell you that something is wrong; tests of synthesis (albumin, INR) tell you how well the liver is working. A patient can have enormously raised ALT but a normal INR, or advanced cirrhosis with only modestly raised enzymes and a failing INR.

blocks.title: Not everything in plasma is hepatic
blocks.text: Immunoglobulins are made by plasma cells, not hepatocytes, so gamma globulins may actually be raised in chronic liver disease. Do not call all clotting problems 'liver failure': vitamin K deficiency also prolongs the INR, but it corrects with vitamin K whereas synthetic failure does not.

points: The liver processes all portal blood: it stores glycogen, makes glucose, ketones, VLDL and urea, and detoxifies drugs and hormones by phase I and phase II reactions.

It synthesises albumin (oncotic pressure, half-life about 20 days) and most clotting factors (factor VII half-life about 6 hours), so low albumin causes oedema and ascites and low clotting factors cause bleeding.
ALT and AST indicate hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT indicate cholestasis, and albumin and INR indicate synthetic capacity.
Prolonged INR corrects with vitamin K in deficiency but not in hepatocellular failure.

questions.stem: Which pair of tests best reflects the liver's synthetic capacity?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both depend on hepatocytes making albumin and clotting factors.
distractorRationale.b: These are released from injured hepatocytes; they measure damage, not capacity.
distractorRationale.c: These rise in cholestasis and biliary disease.
distractorRationale.d: These are renal function tests; urea synthesis is hepatic but urea and creatinine are not standard synthetic tests.

questions.explanation: Albumin and the INR depend directly on how much protein the hepatocytes can make. ALT/AST report cell injury and ALP/GGT report cholestasis, so they say little about capacity.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents after paracetamol overdose. ALT is about 40 times the upper reference limit, ALP is normal and INR is 1.1. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Acute hepatocellular injury so far without major loss of synthetic function

questions.correctOptionText: Acute hepatocellular injury so far without major loss of synthetic function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ALT leaks from damaged hepatocytes, while a normal INR shows synthesis is preserved at this time.
distractorRationale.b: Cholestasis would raise ALP and GGT more than ALT.
distractorRationale.c: A normal INR argues against synthetic failure; note the INR can rise later.
distractorRationale.d: Bone disease raises ALP, not ALT.

questions.explanation: A marked ALT rise with normal ALP indicates a hepatocellular pattern. The INR of 1.1 means synthetic function is still preserved, but because injury can progress, serial INR measurement is used to follow the course.

questions.stem: In acute liver failure, why does the prothrombin time lengthen within a day or two while serum albumin remains close to normal?

options.text: Clotting factors such as factor VII have short half-lives, whereas albumin has a half-life of about 20 days
Albumin is made by Kupffer cells, which are spared
Albumin synthesis is independent of hepatocytes
The prothrombin time measures platelets, which fall rapidly

questions.correctOptionText: Clotting factors such as factor VII have short half-lives, whereas albumin has a half-life of about 20 days

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rapid turnover makes clotting factors fall first.
distractorRationale.b: Albumin is made by hepatocytes, not Kupffer cells.
distractorRationale.c: Hepatocytes are the site of albumin synthesis.
distractorRationale.d: Prothrombin time tests clotting factors, not platelet count.

questions.explanation: When synthesis stops, a protein's concentration falls according to its half-life. Factor VII (about 6 hours) falls within hours and lengthens the prothrombin time, but albumin (about 20 days) changes only over weeks.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factor does NOT require vitamin K for its synthesis in the liver?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: factor V is synthesised without vitamin K-dependent carboxylation.
distractorRationale.b: Prothrombin needs vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation.

questions.explanation: Factors II, VII, IX and X are gamma-carboxylated in a vitamin K-dependent step. Factor V is not, which is why a low factor V suggests true hepatocellular failure rather than vitamin K deficiency.

questions.stem: The urea cycle, which converts ammonia to urea, takes place in the liver.
questions.explanation: The complete urea cycle is expressed in hepatocytes. When liver function fails, ammonia is not converted to urea efficiently and accumulates, contributing to hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Factor VII has a plasma half-life of 6 hours. After a toxic insult, hepatic synthesis of factor VII stops completely. Assuming first-order decay and no other losses, what percentage of the starting factor VII activity remains after 18 hours?
questions.explanation: 18 hours is 18/6 = 3 half-lives, so the remaining fraction is (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%. This shows why the prothrombin time becomes prolonged within a day of synthesis failing.

questions.stem: A fasting 70 kg adult stores 100 g of liver glycogen. Assume hepatic glucose output is 2 mg per kg body mass per minute and that all of it comes from glycogenolysis. How many hours does the glycogen last?
questions.explanation: Output is 2 mg/kg/min x 70 kg = 140 mg/min = 8.4 g/h. Time = 100 g / 8.4 g/h = 11.9 hours. In reality gluconeogenesis contributes increasingly during fasting, which is why the liver provides glucose well beyond this time.

questions.stem: A man with advanced cirrhosis has pitting ankle oedema, ascites and easy bruising. Explain how reduced hepatic synthetic function accounts for these findings.
markingGuide: The liver synthesises albumin, which provides most of plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure
Low albumin reduces oncotic pressure so fluid leaves capillaries into the interstitium and peritoneal cavity (oedema, ascites); portal hypertension also contributes
The liver synthesises most clotting factors (fibrinogen, II, V, VII, IX, X)
Reduced clotting factors prolong the prothrombin time/INR and cause bruising and bleeding
Factor VII has a short half-life so clotting changes appear early; albumin has a half-life of about 20 days so falls more slowly
questions.explanation: The three signs share one cause: export proteins are no longer made in adequate amounts. Albumin loss shifts Starling forces towards fluid leaving vessels, while clotting factor loss impairs haemostasis.

questions.stem: Explain how you would use albumin, INR, ALT and ALP to distinguish hepatocellular injury, cholestasis and impaired synthetic function. State which test is a faster and which a slower marker of synthesis, and why.
markingGuide: ALT (and AST) are enzymes released from damaged hepatocytes, so a marked rise indicates hepatocellular injury
ALP (and GGT) rise in cholestasis or biliary injury; ALP can also come from bone so GGT helps confirm hepatic origin
Albumin and INR reflect synthetic function rather than injury
INR is the faster marker because factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours
Albumin is the slower marker because its half-life is about 20 days; it is also affected by nutrition, inflammation and protein loss
A normal INR does not exclude severe injury early on and reference ranges vary by laboratory
questions.explanation: Each test samples a different process: leakage, canalicular export, or protein production. Interpreting them together, and knowing their time courses, avoids mistaking acute damage for chronic failure.

questions.stem: Group the liver's functions under metabolic, synthetic, detoxification and storage headings, giving one example under each, and state one consequence of failure of the detoxification function.
markingGuide: Metabolic: glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, VLDL assembly or deamination and urea formation
Synthetic: albumin or clotting factors or transport proteins
Detoxification: cytochrome P450 phase I oxidation and phase II conjugation of drugs and hormones; ammonia to urea
Storage: glycogen, iron or fat-soluble vitamins
Consequence of detoxification failure: ammonia accumulation (hepatic encephalopathy), prolonged drug effects or hormone excess
questions.explanation: Grouping functions by type helps predict what fails in a given disease. For example, loss of the urea cycle leads to hyperammonaemia, and impaired phase I/II metabolism prolongs the action of many drugs.
